one_liner: Patched Lua 5.4.3 plus a bytecode-to-C compiler (luaot); compiled modules ran 1.2x to 2.6x faster than the stock interpreter.
what_it_does: LuaAOT is a modified Lua 5.4.3 (interpreter and liblua) with an extra luaot tool that turns a Lua source file into a C file exporting luaopen_<name>. You build that C file with gcc -O2 against the LuaAOT headers into a .so for require, or with -e into a standalone executable linked to liblua.a. Scripts need no changes and keep full Lua 5.4 semantics, but compiled modules only run on the LuaAOT build of Lua, not on stock Lua.
how_it_is_fast: The compiler partially evaluates the reference interpreter: each Lua function becomes one C function, each bytecode becomes a labelled block holding that opcode's interpreter code with the instruction word baked in as a constant, and Lua jumps become C gotos. This removes fetch-and-dispatch, and gcc can constant-fold the immediate operands and drop dead branches. A patched luaV_execute runs a trampoline loop: compiled functions return the next CallInfo instead of recursing, which keeps coroutines, tail calls and debug hooks working.
when_to_use: You embed Lua 5.4 in a C or C++ host and need its semantics (integers, bitwise operators, goto, to-be-closed variables), which rules out LuaJIT's 5.1 dialect.
Platforms that forbid runtime code generation (W^X or app-store rules) but allow shipping native code built ahead of time.
Numeric, loop-heavy scripts: fannkuch, mandelbrot and spectralnorm ran 2.0x to 2.6x faster than Lua 5.4.3.
Shipping a fixed set of Lua modules or a single-file executable (luaot -e) where a build step per script is acceptable.
when_not_to_use: When LuaJIT is allowed: it was 2.4x to 31x faster than Lua on the same runs. Even LuaJIT with the JIT off (-joff) beat LuaAOT on 4 of 7 programs (binarytrees 1.91 s vs 2.68 s, fasta 3.02 vs 3.84, knucleotide 2.28 vs 3.44, nbody 8.92 vs 12.14; derived from page data).
Allocation-, string- or table-heavy code, where the gain was only 1.21x to 1.32x (binarytrees, fasta, knucleotide).

Large code bases: issue #13 reports Teal (11,012 Lua lines) becoming about 600,000 lines of C that took 28.7 s and 6.7 GB peak memory to compile, and issue #11 reports about 200 KB extra memory per compiled module versus 5-15 KB for the plain one.
Projects that need current Lua: the base is 5.4.3, without the 5.4.4+ bug fixes or 5.5. There has been no commit since 2023-12-06, and there is no test suite (issue #3 open).
Builds that would use the switch-based trampoline compiler (luaot-trampoline): it gave only 0.99x to 1.48x over Lua 5.4.3 (derived from page data).

integration.form: Modified Lua 5.4.3 (static liblua.a and lua binary) plus the luaot compiler; generated C is built as a shared module or an executable
integration.dependencies: none beyond a C compiler and libc/libm (dlopen for .so modules)
integration.min_toolchain: C99 (src/Makefile uses gcc -std=gnu99 -O2); compile generated modules with at least -O2 per the README
integration.platforms: Whatever Lua 5.4.3's 'make guess' supports (Linux, macOS, other POSIX); the experiments ran on Linux x86-64
integration.thread_safety: Same as Lua (one lua_State per thread). A module's luaopen_ function mutates a file-static counter, so it is not safe to call concurrently or more than once per process.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — same language and public C API as Lua 5.4.3, but the host must link the LuaAOT-patched interpreter (Proto gains an aot_implementation field and internal APIs are exported), and compiled modules load only into that build

gotchas: Bug in the generated loader (src/luaot_footer.c): bind_magic takes function pointers from LUAOT_FUNCTIONS[next_id++], where next_id is a file-static counter that is never reset. Calling luaopen_<module> a second time in the same process (a second lua_State, or require after clearing package.loaded) starts past the end of the array. The main chunk silently falls back to the interpreter on the trailing NULL, and nested functions get out-of-bounds pointers, which is undefined behaviour and a likely crash. Multi-state C++ hosts are affected; the single-process benchmarks are not.

The module embeds the original Lua source and re-parses it with luaL_loadbuffer at load time, then binds compiled functions by traversal order. Load errors call exit(1) instead of raising a Lua error, the source ships readable inside the .so, and issue #19 reports that files starting with a shebang fail to run.

Undated benchmark data: statistics/times-slow.txt has seven columns (lua, lsw, aot, cor, trm, jof, jit), but the current scripts/bench-run.lua only produces five. Per statistics/plot.r, the paper's 'LuaAOT' is the 'cor' column, while 'aot' (an earlier variant) gives 1.22x to 2.25x, not 2.64x, on mandelbrot.

LuaJIT rows ran slightly different source on 3 of 7 programs (binarytrees_jit, fasta_jit and mandelbrot_jit use 2^, the bit library and math.floor in place of 5.4 operators). Use only knucleotide and nbody when comparing LuaJIT's interpreter with LuaAOT on identical code.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick LuaAOT over LuaJIT only when you must stay on Lua 5.4 semantics or cannot JIT and your hot code is numeric loops; otherwise LuaJIT, even with its JIT off, is as fast or faster. It is the Lua counterpart of Lightstorm (mruby AOT, about 30% less time): the same no-dispatch compile-the-interpreter idea, with larger gains here on numeric code.
verified_claims_summary: The repo's statistics/times-slow.txt has 20 wall-clock runs per cell (/usr/bin/time -p on the whole process, output to /dev/null) on an unnamed x86-64 CPU at about 3.06 GHz (perf counters), with gcc -O2 and a gcc version not stated. Against the stock Lua 5.4.3 interpreter, the paper's LuaAOT variant took 1.21x (knucleotide) to 2.64x (mandelbrot) less time; I recomputed all seven means from the raw file and they match the record. The SBLP 2021 paper reports 20% to 60% shorter run times (abstract seen as a search snippet only).
status_note: Stale research artefact from PUC-Rio (last commit 2023-12-06, 91 commits, 165 stars), MIT-licensed and small (luaot.c plus its goto-mode opcode template is about 1,600 lines of C), so it can be vendored. You would own rebasing onto a newer Lua 5.4.x and fixing the luaopen re-entry bug.
